title: Πυγμαχία
titleEn: Nestor’s Gift and the Boxing — Iliad 23.586–699
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The quarrel over the second prize ends at once. Antilochus asks Menelaus to bear with a young man’s rashness and offers him the mare he won; Menelaus, cheered, gives way, praises Antilochus for the toil he and his family have borne for him, and hands the mare back. The remaining prizes are given out, and Achilles presents the last, a bowl of a kind the Greek does not let us name, to the old Nestor as a memorial of Patroclus. Nestor thanks him, wishing for his lost strength and recalling his victories at the funeral of Amarynceus. Then the boxing begins: Achilles sets a mule against a double cup, the braggart Epeius claims the mule and threatens his opponent, and only Euryalus stands up to him. Diomedes arms him, but one blow from Epeius ends the fight.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίλοχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Antilochos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Antilochus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Antilochus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: Antilochus answers Menelaus, whose speech ended the last part. The whole line is a reply formula: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ ‘to him in turn’ (τόν is the article used as a pronoun), then the speaker, then ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’ (ἀντίον is an adverb ‘facing’; ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’). πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is the perfect participle of πέπνυμαι ‘have sense’. His speech runs to line 595.

sentences.t: ἄνσχεο νῦν·
sentences.tr: anscheo nyn·
sentences.l: “Hold out now;
sentences.i: “Bear up now;
sentences.n: ἄνσχεο is the aorist imperative of the middle ἀνέχομαι ‘hold oneself up, put up with’, and here it is an order to hold back anger. Antilochus has just been accused of cheating, and he begins by asking Menelaus to calm down. νῦν ‘now’ marks the moment.

sentences.t:
πολλὸν γὰρ ἔγωγε νεώτερός εἰμι
σεῖο ἄναξ Μενέλαε, σὺ δὲ πρότερος καὶ ἀρείων.
sentences.tr:
pollon gar egōge neōteros eimi
seio anax Menelae, sy de proteros kai areiōn.
sentences.l:
for much younger am I
than you, lord Menelaus, and you are elder and better.
sentences.i: for I am much younger than you, lord Menelaus, and you are elder and better.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the order. νεώτερος is the comparative of νέος ‘young’, and σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’ (the genitive of comparison). ἄναξ ‘lord’ is the vocative. πρότερος is ‘elder’ (in age) and ἀρείων ‘better’; the same two words stand side by side at 2.707, where the sense is ‘braver’, but here the contrast is of age and standing, so ‘better’ is used.

sentences.t: οἶσθ’ οἷαι νέου ἀνδρὸς ὑπερβασίαι τελέθουσι·
sentences.tr: oisth’ hoiai neou andros hyperbasiai telethousi·
sentences.l: You know what sort of oversteppings a young man’s are;
sentences.i: You know what a young man’s transgressions are like;
sentences.n: οἶσθ’ is οἶσθα, the perfect of οἶδα ‘know’ with present sense. οἷαι ‘of what sort’ introduces the clause, and ὑπερβασίαι is ‘oversteppings’, from ὑπερβαίνω ‘step over’: going beyond what is proper (the Odyssey has the same noun). τελέθουσι is a poetic plural for ‘are’, agreeing with ὑπερβασίαι. Antilochus excuses himself by his youth.

sentences.t: κραιπνότερος μὲν γάρ τε νόος, λεπτὴ δέ τε μῆτις.
sentences.tr: kraipnoteros men gar te noos, leptē de te mētis.
sentences.l: for more rushing is the mind, and thin the cunning.
sentences.i: for the mind is more rushing, and the cunning thin.
sentences.n: κραιπνότερος is the comparative of κραιπνός ‘rushing’, agreeing with νόος ‘mind’; μὲν … δέ sets ‘more rushing’ against ‘thin’, and the τε after γάρ and after δέ marks a general truth. λεπτή ‘thin’ goes with μῆτις ‘cunning’. The half-line λεπτὴ δέ τε μῆτις also stands at 10.226.

sentences.t: τώ τοι ἐπιτλήτω κραδίη·
sentences.tr: tō toi epitlētō kradiē·
sentences.l: Therefore let your heart endure;
sentences.i: So let your heart endure it;
sentences.n: τώ is the epic form of τῷ ‘therefore’. τοι is the epic dative of σύ, ‘for you’. ἐπιτλήτω is the aorist imperative, third person, of ἐπιτλῆναι ‘endure, bear’, and κραδίη is the epic form of καρδία ‘heart’. He asks Menelaus’ heart to bear the offence, and offers amends in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἵππον δέ τοι αὐτὸς
δώσω, τὴν ἀρόμην.
sentences.tr:
hippon de toi autos
dōsō, tēn aromēn.
sentences.l:
and a horse to you myself
I shall give, the one that I won.
sentences.i: And I will give you a horse myself, the one I won.
sentences.n: δώσω is the future of δίδωμι ‘give’, and αὐτός ‘myself’ stresses that the gift is his own. τήν is feminine, so the horse is a mare, the prize he won; ἀρόμην is the aorist of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, without the augment. The mare is the one in dispute, and he offers it to Menelaus outright.

sentences.t:
εἰ καί νύ κεν οἴκοθεν ἄλλο
μεῖζον ἐπαιτήσειας,
sentences.tr:
ei kai ny ken oikothen allo
meizon epaitēseias,
sentences.l:
Even if indeed anything else
greater from my house you were to ask besides,
sentences.i: And even if you were to ask for something else, something greater, from my house,
sentences.n: εἰ καί … κεν with the aorist optative ἐπαιτήσειας means ‘even if you were to ask’; the main clause follows in the next unit. ἐπαιτέω is ‘ask in addition’, and οἴκοθεν ‘from home’ has the suffix -θεν ‘from’. ἄλλο μεῖζον is ‘something else, greater’; νύ is a small particle of emphasis.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ κέ τοι αὐτίκα δοῦναι
βουλοίμην ἢ σοί γε διοτρεφὲς ἤματα πάντα
ἐκ θυμοῦ πεσέειν καὶ δαίμοσιν εἶναι ἀλιτρός.
sentences.tr:
aphar ke toi autika dounai
bouloimēn ē soi ge diotrephes ēmata panta
ek thymou peseein kai daimosin einai alitros.
sentences.l:
straightway to you forthwith to give
I would wish, rather than that for you, Zeus-nurtured one, for all my days
from your spirit to fall and to the gods be sinful.”
sentences.i: I would be willing to give it to you at once, right away, rather than fall out of your heart for all my days, Zeus-nurtured one, and be sinful before the gods.”
sentences.n: The main clause. ἄφαρ ‘at once’ and αὐτίκα ‘straightway’ pile up for emphasis. δοῦναι is the aorist infinitive of δίδωμι, and βουλοίμην the optative of βούλομαι ‘wish’; βούλομαι … ἤ means ‘would rather … than’, and ‘it’ (the greater thing) is understood. διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ is a vocative, as at 23.581. ἐκ θυμοῦ πεσέειν is ‘to fall out of [your] spirit’, to lose his regard (πεσέειν is the epic aorist infinitive of πίπτω). δαίμοσιν is the dative plural of δαίμων ‘divinity’, and ἀλιτρός ‘sinful’ is an offender, ‘to the gods’ is ‘in the gods’ eyes’. ἤματα πάντα ‘all my days’ is an accusative of time. His speech ends.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἵππον ἄγων μεγαθύμου Νέστορος υἱὸς
ἐν χείρεσσι τίθει Μενελάου·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai hippon agōn megathymou Nestoros huios
en cheiressi tithei Menelaou·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and leading the horse, the son of great-hearted Nestor
put it into the hands of Menelaus;
sentences.i: So he said, and the son of great-hearted Nestor led the horse up and put it into Menelaus’ hands;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes a speech. The son of Nestor is Antilochus, not named. ἄγων ‘leading’ goes with ἵππον, and τίθει is the unaugmented imperfect (= ἐτίθει) ‘put’; ἐν χείρεσσι is ‘into the hands’, with the epic dative plural -εσσι. Μενελάου is the genitive of Μενέλαος.

sentences.t:
τοῖο δὲ θυμὸς
ἰάνθη ὡς εἴ τε περὶ σταχύεσσιν ἐέρση
ληΐου ἀλδήσκοντος, ὅτε φρίσσουσιν ἄρουραι·
sentences.tr:
toio de thymos
ianthē hōs ei te peri stachyessin eersē
lēïou aldēskontos, hote phrissousin arourai·
sentences.i: and his spirit was cheered, as dew cheers the ears of a growing crop when the plough-lands bristle;
sentences.n: τοῖο is the epic genitive of the article used as a pronoun, ‘his’, Menelaus’. ἰάνθη is the aorist passive of ἰαίνω ‘warm’, used of a heart for ‘cheer’; the comparison is the dew on the ears of corn. ὡς εἴ τε begins the simile and the verb is left to be supplied from ἰάνθη, which is why the English says ‘cheers’. ληΐου ἀλδήσκοντος is ‘of the crop as it grows’ (ἀλδήσκω ‘grow’); φρίσσουσιν ἄρουραι is ‘the plough-lands bristle’ with ripening ears.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα σοὶ Μενέλαε μετὰ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἰάνθη.
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara soi Menelae meta phresi thymos ianthē.
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So then, Menelaus, in your wits your spirit was warmed.
And, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So, Menelaus, was your spirit cheered within you. And lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: The poet turns to Menelaus with σοί ‘for you’ and the vocative Μενέλαε, and closes the simile with ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’; μετὰ φρεσί is ‘among the wits’, within him. The second line is the usual speech introduction: φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’ and ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, with προσηύδα ‘he spoke to’. Here μιν is Antilochus, and the speaker is Menelaus.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχε νῦν μέν τοι ἐγὼν ὑποείξομαι αὐτὸς
χωόμενος,
sentences.tr:
Antiloche nyn men toi egōn hypoeixomai autos
chōomenos,
sentences.l:
“Antilochus, now to you I myself shall give way,
being incensed,
sentences.i: “Antilochus, now I myself will give way to you, incensed though I am,
sentences.n: Menelaus gives way. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ὑποείξομαι is the future middle of ὑπείκω ‘give way’, with the epic extra ο, and αὐτός ‘myself’ says that he yields of his own accord. χωόμενος ‘incensed’ is a participle with the sense ‘though I am incensed’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὔ τι παρήορος οὐδ’ ἀεσίφρων
ἦσθα πάρος·
sentences.tr:
epei ou ti parēoros oud’ aesiphrōn
ēstha paros·
sentences.l:
since not at all swung-aside nor senseless
were you before;
sentences.i: since before now you were neither one to swing aside nor senseless;
sentences.n: Menelaus says why he yields: Antilochus has not behaved like this before. ἦσθα is the imperfect of εἰμί, ‘you were’, and πάρος ‘before’. παρήορος is built on παρά ‘beside’ and ἀείρω ‘lift, swing’; its sense here is not known for certain, and the English keeps its parts (it is the word for the outer horse yoked beside the pair at 16.471). ἀεσίφρων ‘senseless’ is also uncertain in origin.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτε νόον νίκησε νεοίη.
sentences.tr: nyn aute noon nikēse neoiē.
sentences.l: now in turn youthfulness prevailed over your mind.
sentences.i: but this time youth has defeated your mind.
sentences.n: νεοίη ‘youthfulness’ is an abstract noun from νέος ‘young’, and it is the subject; νόον ‘mind’ is the object of νίκησε, the aorist of νικάω. νῦν αὖτε ‘now, in turn’ sets this time against πάρος ‘before’. Menelaus echoes Antilochus’ own account of the young man’s mind at 590.

sentences.t: δεύτερον αὖτ’ ἀλέασθαι ἀμείνονας ἠπεροπεύειν.
sentences.tr: deuteron aut’ aleasthai ameinonas ēperopeuein.
sentences.l: A second time, in turn, avoid deceiving better men.
sentences.i: Next time, avoid deceiving your betters.
sentences.n: ἀλέασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid, steer clear of’, used as an order, and its object is the infinitive ἠπεροπεύειν ‘to deceive’. ἀμείνονας is the accusative plural of ἀμείνων ‘better’, ‘better men’. δεύτερον is adverbial, ‘a second time’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ κέν με τάχ’ ἄλλος ἀνὴρ παρέπεισεν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: ou gar ken me tach’ allos anēr parepeisen Achaiōn.
sentences.l: For not quickly would another man of the Achaeans have persuaded me over.
sentences.i: For no other of the Achaeans would so quickly have won me over.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ gives the reason: Antilochus is the one man who could do it. κεν with the aorist indicative παρέπεισεν gives ‘would have’. παραπείθω is ‘win over’, literally ‘persuade aside’, and τάχα here is ‘quickly’. ἄλλος ἀνὴρ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘another man of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ γὰρ δὴ πολλὰ πάθες καὶ πολλὰ μόγησας
σός τε πατὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ἀδελφεὸς εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο·
sentences.tr:
alla sy gar dē polla pathes kai polla mogēsas
sos te patēr agathos kai adelpheos heinek’ emeio·
sentences.l:
But you, for you have indeed suffered much and toiled much,
both your father, a good one, and your brother, for my sake;
sentences.i: But you have suffered much and toiled much for my sake, and so has your good father, and your brother;
sentences.n: The reason Menelaus gives for his generosity. πάθες and μόγησας are aorists (πάθες for ἔπαθες) of πάσχω ‘suffer’ and μογέω ‘toil’. σός τε πατὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ἀδελφεός adds two more subjects to the same verbs: ἀγαθός stands after πατήρ, so it may go with the brother too. εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο is ‘for my sake’ (ἐμεῖο, epic genitive of ἐγώ). The brother is not named.

sentences.t: τώ τοι λισσομένῳ ἐπιπείσομαι,
sentences.tr: tō toi lissomenōi epipeisomai,
sentences.l: Therefore to you, entreating, I shall comply,
sentences.i: So I will comply with your entreaty,
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’ (as at 591). λισσομένῳ is the dative participle of λίσσομαι ‘entreat’, agreeing with τοι ‘to you’, and ἐπιπείσομαι is the future of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey, comply with’. Antilochus asked him to bear up (587) and he agrees.

sentences.t:
ἠδὲ καὶ ἵππον
δώσω ἐμήν περ ἐοῦσαν,
sentences.tr:
ēde kai hippon
dōsō emēn per eousan,
sentences.l:
and also the horse
I shall give, though it is mine,
sentences.i: and I will give you the horse as well, though it is mine,
sentences.n: ἠδὲ καί ‘and also’. The mare is the one Antilochus has just put into his hands, and the τοι ‘to you’ of the line before still serves as the receiver of δώσω ‘I shall give’. ἐμήν περ ἐοῦσαν is a feminine participle, ‘though she is mine’, with περ ‘though’: the mare is Menelaus’ now, and he gives it back.

sentences.t:
ἵνα γνώωσι καὶ οἵδε
ὡς ἐμὸς οὔ ποτε θυμὸς ὑπερφίαλος καὶ ἀπηνής.
sentences.tr:
hina gnōōsi kai hoide
hōs emos ou pote thymos hyperphialos kai apēnēs.
sentences.l:
so that these too may know
that my spirit is never overweening and unkind.”
sentences.i: so that these men here may also know that my spirit is never overweening or unkind.”
sentences.n: ἵνα with the aorist subjunctive γνώωσι (epic for γνῶσι) ‘so that they may know’. καὶ οἵδε ‘these also’ points to the Argive leaders standing round, whom he addressed at 573. ὡς introduces what they are to know, and the verb ‘is’ is left out. ὑπερφίαλος ‘overweening’ and ἀπηνής ‘unkind’ (its origin is not known) both describe θυμός ‘spirit’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ Ἀντιλόχοιο Νοήμονι δῶκεν ἑταίρῳ
ἵππον ἄγειν·
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai Antilochoio Noēmoni dōken hetairōi
hippon agein·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and to Noemon, the companion of Antilochus, gave
the horse to lead away;
sentences.i: So he said, and gave the horse to Antilochus’ companion Noemon to lead away;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes the speech. The giver is Menelaus, who is not named; Noemon is Antilochus’ companion, both in the dative (Νοήμονι … ἑταίρῳ), and Ἀντιλόχοιο is the epic genitive. ἄγειν is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to lead’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα λέβηθ’ ἕλε παμφανόωντα.
sentences.tr: ho d’ epeita lebēth’ hele pamphanoōnta.
sentences.l: and he then took the all-shining cauldron.
sentences.i: and he then took the all-shining cauldron.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Menelaus, who now takes his own prize, the cauldron that was third (23.267); Antilochus keeps the mare, which was the second. λέβηθ’ is λέβητα with the final vowel dropped and τ made θ before the rough breathing of ἕλε. ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’. A cauldron is one of the prizes listed at 23.264–270. παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’ is the uncontracted epic form.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ ἀνάειρε δύω χρυσοῖο τάλαντα
τέτρατος, ὡς ἔλασεν.
sentences.tr:
Mērionēs d’ anaeire dyō chrysoio talanta
tetratos, hōs elasen.
sentences.l:
And Meriones lifted two talents of gold,
fourth, as he had driven.
sentences.i: And Meriones, who came fourth in the driving, lifted two talents of gold.
sentences.n: ἀνάειρε is a past tense of ἀείρω ‘lift’ (ἀνά ‘up’), and δύω … τάλαντα is ‘two talents’; as at 23.269 the weight of a Homeric talent is not known. τέτρατος ‘fourth’ agrees with Μηριόνης, and ὡς ἔλασεν (aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’) is ‘as he drove’, that is, in the order of his finish.

sentences.t:
πέμπτον δ’ ὑπελείπετ’ ἄεθλον,
ἀμφίθετος φιάλη·
sentences.tr:
pempton d’ hypeleipet’ aethlon,
amphithetos phialē·
sentences.l:
and a fifth contest-prize was left over,
a bowl, a both-sides-set one;
sentences.i: A fifth prize was left over, a bowl of the ‘both-sides-set’ kind;
sentences.n: ὑπελείπετ’ is the imperfect passive of ὑπολείπω ‘leave behind’, ‘was left over’. πέμπτον ‘fifth’ goes with ἄεθλον ‘prize’ (the prize, not the contest). ἀμφίθετος is built on ἀμφί ‘on both sides’ and θετός ‘set’, and its meaning is not known; it describes the φιάλη ‘bowl’ at 23.270 too, and the English keeps its parts.

sentences.t:
τὴν Νέστορι δῶκεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
Ἀργείων ἀν’ ἀγῶνα φέρων, καὶ ἔειπε παραστάς·
sentences.tr:
tēn Nestori dōken Achilleus
Argeiōn an’ agōna pherōn, kai eeipe parastas·
sentences.l:
which to Nestor gave Achilles,
carrying it up through the gathering of the Argives, and he spoke, standing beside him:
sentences.i: Achilles carried it through the gathering of the Argives and gave it to Nestor, and said, standing at his side:
sentences.n: τήν ‘this one’ is the feminine article used as a pronoun, picking up φιάλη. ἀν’ is ἀνά ‘up, through’ with the accusative ἀγῶνα; ἀγών is ‘gathering’, the place where the people sit. φέρων ‘carrying’, ἔειπε ‘spoke’ (aorist of εἶπον), and παραστάς ‘standing beside’ (aorist participle of παρίστημι).

sentences.t:
τῆ νῦν, καὶ σοὶ τοῦτο γέρον κειμήλιον ἔστω
Πατρόκλοιο τάφου μνῆμ’ ἔμμεναι·
sentences.tr:
tē nyn, kai soi touto geron keimēlion estō
Patrokloio taphou mnēm’ emmenai·
sentences.l:
“Here, take it now, and let this be a treasure for you too, old man,
to be a memorial of the burial of Patroclus;
sentences.i: “Here, take this now, and let it be a treasure for you too, old man, to be a memorial of Patroclus’ burial;
sentences.n: τῆ is a word used when handing something over, ‘here, take’. κειμήλιον ‘treasure’ is a thing laid up (from κεῖμαι ‘lie’). ἔστω is the third-person imperative, and ἔμμεναι the epic infinitive of εἰμί, ‘to be’. μνῆμα is ‘memorial’, and τάφου is the genitive of τάφος ‘burial’ (a different word from the τάφος ‘amazement’ of the Odyssey). γέρον is the vocative, ‘old man’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ αὐτὸν
ὄψῃ ἐν Ἀργείοισι·
sentences.tr:
ou gar et’ auton
opsēi en Argeioisi·
sentences.l:
for no longer him himself
will you see among the Argives;
sentences.i: for you will not see him in person among the Argives any more;
sentences.n: ὄψῃ is the epic future of ὁράω, ‘you will see’, second singular. αὐτόν ‘him himself’ is Patroclus in person, as against the keepsake that stands for him; Ἀργείοισι is the epic dative plural of Ἀργεῖοι. The reason for the gift: the bowl must stand in the place of the man.

sentences.t:
δίδωμι δέ τοι τόδ’ ἄεθλον
αὔτως·
sentences.tr:
didōmi de toi tod’ aethlon
autōs·
sentences.l:
and I give you this contest-prize
just so;
sentences.i: and I give you this prize without more ado;
sentences.n: δίδωμι ‘I give’ is a present, and τόδ’ ἄεθλον is ‘this prize’. αὔτως ‘just so’ here means with no contest; the reason follows in the next lines.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πύξ γε μαχήσεαι, οὐδὲ παλαίσεις,
οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀκοντιστὺν ἐσδύσεαι, οὐδὲ πόδεσσι
θεύσεαι·
sentences.tr:
ou gar pyx ge machēseai, oude palaiseis,
oud’ et’ akontistyn esdyseai, oude podessi
theuseai·
sentences.i: for you will not box, or wrestle, or take part in the javelin-throwing again, or run a race on foot;
sentences.n: Four futures in the second singular: μαχήσεαι (the epic -εαι), παλαίσεις ‘wrestle’, ἐσδύσεαι (= εἰσδύσεαι, ‘go into’, enter a contest) and θεύσεαι ‘run’ (θέω). πύξ is an adverb ‘with the fist’. ἀκοντιστύν is the accusative of ἀκοντιστύς ‘javelin-throwing’, from ἀκοντίζω ‘cast’. οὐδ’ ἔτι ‘not again, no longer’.

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ χαλεπὸν κατὰ γῆρας ἐπείγει.
sentences.tr: ēdē gar chalepon kata gēras epeigei.
sentences.l: for already harsh old age presses down.”
sentences.i: for harsh old age is already pressing hard on you.”
sentences.n: κατὰ … ἐπείγει is tmesis (the preposition separated from its verb) for κατεπείγω ‘press down on, weigh upon’. χαλεπὸν γῆρας ‘harsh old age’ is the subject. The sentence gives the reason for all the denials in the line before. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χερσὶ τίθει· ὃ δ’ ἐδέξατο χαίρων,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn en chersi tithei· ho d’ edexato chairōn,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So speaking, into his hands he put it; and he received it, rejoicing,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: With these words he put it into his hands, and he took it gladly, and lifting his voice spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so speaking’; τίθει is the unaugmented imperfect, as at 597. ὃ δ’ (Nestor) ἐδέξατο, the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’, with χαίρων ‘rejoicing’. The second line is the usual introduction: φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’. Here μιν is Achilles.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα τέκος κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge panta tekos kata moiran eeipes·
sentences.l: “Yes, indeed, all this, at least, child, according to what is fitting you have spoken.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, child, all this you have said, as is fitting.
sentences.n: Nestor thanks him. ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’; ταῦτά γε πάντα ‘all this, at least’; τέκος is ‘child’, an old man’s address to the younger. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’, μοῖρα being a due portion, and ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον. The same line is spoken in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔμπεδα γυῖα φίλος πόδες, οὐδέ τι χεῖρες
ὤμων ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἐπαΐσσονται ἐλαφραί.
sentences.tr:
ou gar et’ empeda guia philos podes, oude ti cheires
ōmōn amphoterōthen epaïssontai elaphrai.
sentences.l:
for no longer are my limbs firm, friend, my feet, nor do my hands
from the shoulders on both sides dart out, light.
sentences.i: for no longer are my limbs firm, friend, my feet, and my hands no longer dart out lightly from my shoulders on either side.
sentences.n: The edition prints no commas round φίλος. φίλος cannot agree with the neuter γυῖα ‘limbs’ or the plural πόδες ‘feet’, so it is taken as a vocative, ‘friend’; πόδες is in apposition to γυῖα. ἔμπεδα is ‘firm’. ἐπαΐσσονται ‘dart out’ takes ὤμων ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘from the shoulders on both sides’, and ἐλαφραί ‘light’ agrees with χεῖρες ‘hands’. He is describing the arms swinging free of the shoulders in a boxer or thrower.

sentences.t:
εἴθ’ ὣς ἡβώοιμι βίη τέ μοι ἔμπεδος εἴη
ὡς ὁπότε κρείοντ’ Ἀμαρυγκέα θάπτον Ἐπειοὶ
Βουπρασίῳ, παῖδες δ’ ἔθεσαν βασιλῆος ἄεθλα·
sentences.tr:
eith’ hōs hēbōoimi biē te moi empedos eiē
hōs hopote kreiont’ Amarynkea thapton Epeioi
Bouprasiōi, paides d’ ethesan basilēos aethla·
sentences.i: If only I were as young as that, and my strength were firm, as when the Epeans were burying lord Amarynceus at Buprasium, and the sons of the king set out prizes;
sentences.n: The first line is the same as a line of the Odyssey and, except for τέ in place of δέ, as Iliad 7.157 and 11.670; the English follows the Iliad’s ‘young’ for ἡβώοιμι (ἡβάω ‘be in youthful prime’). εἴθε with the optative is a wish, here for a strength he no longer has. ὡς ὁπότε ‘as when’ starts the memory: κρείοντ’ Ἀμαρυγκέα is ‘lord Amarynceus’ (accusative), θάπτον ‘were burying’ is an imperfect, and Ἐπειοί ‘Epeans’ is the subject, a people. Βουπρασίῳ is a place name. παῖδες … βασιλῆος ‘the sons of the king’ set out the prizes (ἔθεσαν, aorist of τίθημι).

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔ τίς μοι ὁμοῖος ἀνὴρ γένετ’, οὔτ’ ἄρ’ Ἐπειῶν
οὔτ’ αὐτῶν Πυλίων οὔτ’ Αἰτωλῶν μεγαθύμων.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ou tis moi homoios anēr genet’, out’ ar’ Epeiōn
out’ autōn Pyliōn out’ Aitōlōn megathymōn.
sentences.l:
There no man became like me, neither of the Epeans
nor of the Pylians themselves, nor of the great-hearted Aetolians.
sentences.i: There no man came to equal me, either of the Epeans, or of the Pylians themselves, or of the great-hearted Aetolians.
sentences.n: ὁμοῖος with the dative μοι is ‘like me’, and γένετ’ ‘came to be’. οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor … nor’ takes three genitives of the peoples the man might have come from. αὐτῶν Πυλίων ‘the Pylians themselves’ is Nestor’s own people. Αἰτωλῶν is the genitive of Αἰτωλοί ‘Aetolians’.

sentences.t: πὺξ μὲν ἐνίκησα Κλυτομήδεα Ἤνοπος υἱόν,
sentences.tr: pyx men enikēsa Klytomēdea Ēnopos huion,
sentences.l: With the fist I defeated Clytomedes, Enops’ son,
sentences.i: I defeated Clytomedes, son of Enops, with my fists,
sentences.n: Four victories follow (634–637), over five men, in boxing, wrestling, running and the spear throw, with μέν … δέ linking them. πύξ is ‘with the fist’, and ἐνίκησα the aorist of νικάω ‘defeat’. Κλυτομήδεα is the accusative of Κλυτομήδης, and Ἤνοπος the genitive of Ἤνοψ ‘Enops’, whose son he is.

sentences.t: Ἀγκαῖον δὲ πάλῃ Πλευρώνιον, ὅς μοι ἀνέστη·
sentences.tr: Ankaion de palēi Pleurōnion, hos moi anestē·
sentences.l: and Ancaeus the Pleuronian in wrestling, who stood up against me;
sentences.i: and Ancaeus of Pleuron in wrestling, who stood up against me;
sentences.n: πάλῃ is the dative of πάλη ‘wrestling’. Πλευρώνιον ‘the Pleuronian’ names Ancaeus’ town, Pleuron. ὅς is the relative; ἀνέστη is the aorist of ἀνίστημι ‘stand up’ and μοι is ‘against me’: he rose to face him.

sentences.t: Ἴφικλον δὲ πόδεσσι παρέδραμον ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα,
sentences.tr: Iphiklon de podessi paredramon esthlon eonta,
sentences.l: and Iphiclus with my feet I ran past, though he was good,
sentences.i: and I outran Iphiclus, good man though he was,
sentences.n: πόδεσσι ‘with my feet’; παρέδραμον is the aorist of παρατρέχω ‘run past’. ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα is a concessive participle, ‘though being good’ (ἐόντα is the epic form of ὄντα).

sentences.t: δουρὶ δ’ ὑπειρέβαλον Φυλῆά τε καὶ Πολύδωρον.
sentences.tr: douri d’ hypeirebalon Phylēa te kai Polydōron.
sentences.l: and with the spear I threw beyond Phyleus and Polydorus.
sentences.i: and with the spear I threw farther than Phyleus and Polydorus.
sentences.n: ὑπειρέβαλον is the aorist of ὑπερβάλλω ‘throw beyond, surpass’ (the epic form of ὑπερέβαλον), and δουρί ‘with the spear’ gives the event. Φυλῆα is the accusative of Φυλεύς, and the two names are joined by τε καί.

sentences.t:
οἴοισίν μ’ ἵπποισι παρήλασαν Ἀκτορίωνε
πλήθει πρόσθε βαλόντες ἀγασσάμενοι περὶ νίκης,
sentences.tr:
oioisin m’ hippoisi parēlasan Aktoriōne
plēthei prosthe balontes agassamenoi peri nikēs,
sentences.l:
With horses alone they passed me, the two of Actor’s line,
by their numbers throwing themselves ahead, feeling indignation over the victory,
sentences.i: Only with their horses did the pair of Actor’s line get past me, thrusting ahead by their numbers, in indignation over the victory,
sentences.n: οἴοισι ‘alone, only’ goes with ἵπποισι ‘horses’: he was beaten only in the horse race. παρήλασαν is the aorist of παρελαύνω ‘drive past’, and Ἀκτορίωνε is a dual naming the two sons of Actor’s line (2.621). πλήθει ‘by numbers’ and πρόσθε βαλόντες ‘throwing themselves forward’ are hard to place exactly, and the English follows the words. ἀγασσάμενοι is ‘feeling indignation’ (ἀγάομαι either ‘wonder at’ or ‘be indignant’, the sense chosen from the context as at 7.41), and περὶ νίκης ‘over the victory’.

sentences.t: οὕνεκα δὴ τὰ μέγιστα παρ’ αὐτόθι λείπετ’ ἄεθλα.
sentences.tr: houneka dē ta megista par’ autothi leipet’ aethla.
sentences.l: because the greatest contest-prizes were left there on the spot.
sentences.i: because the greatest prizes still remained there.
sentences.n: οὕνεκα ‘because’; τὰ μέγιστα ‘the greatest’ (article with a superlative); παρ’ αὐτόθι ‘right there, on the spot’. λείπετο is the imperfect passive of λείπω, ‘was left, remained’; the Greek does not say for which event, but the sense is that the biggest prizes were still to be won in the chariot race.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔσαν δίδυμοι·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ar’ esan didymoi·
sentences.l: and they were twins;
sentences.i: They were twins:
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ picks up the two of Actor’s line from 638, and ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν ‘they were’. δίδυμοι ‘twins’ is the point, and the line after explains why twins could work as a team.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν ἔμπεδον ἡνιόχευεν,
ἔμπεδον ἡνιόχευ’, ὃ δ’ ἄρα μάστιγι κέλευεν.
sentences.tr:
ho men empedon hēniocheuen,
empedon hēniocheu’, ho d’ ara mastigi keleuen.
sentences.l:
the one drove steadily,
steadily drove, and the other urged on with the whip.
sentences.i: One of them drove steadily, drove steadily, and the other urged the horses on with the whip.
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν … ὃ δέ ‘the one … the other’ (the article as a pronoun). ἔμπεδον is an adverb ‘steadily’, and the poet says it twice. ἡνιόχευεν is the imperfect of ἡνιοχεύω ‘be the charioteer, drive’; μάστιγι is the dative ‘with the whip’, and κέλευεν the imperfect of κελεύω ‘urge on’.

sentences.t: ὥς ποτ’ ἔον·
sentences.tr: hōs pot’ eon·
sentences.l: So once I was;
sentences.i: That is how I once was:
sentences.n: ἔον is the epic imperfect of εἰμί. The same form can be ‘they were’, but the contrast with ἐμὲ δέ in the next line makes it ‘I was’. ὥς ποτε is ‘thus once’, closing the memory.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτε νεώτεροι ἀντιοώντων
ἔργων τοιούτων·
sentences.tr:
nyn aute neōteroi antioōntōn
ergōn toioutōn·
sentences.l:
now in turn let younger men meet
such deeds;
sentences.i: now let younger men meet such deeds;
sentences.n: ἀντιοώντων is the third-person plural imperative of ἀντιάω ‘meet’ (epic form), and the verb takes a genitive, ἔργων τοιούτων ‘such deeds’. νεώτεροι ‘younger men’ is the comparative that Antilochus used of himself at 587. νῦν αὖτε ‘now, in turn’ answers ποτέ.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δὲ χρὴ γήραϊ λυγρῷ
πείθεσθαι,
sentences.tr:
eme de chrē gēraï lygrōi
peithesthai,
sentences.l:
but I must, to grievous old age,
yield,
sentences.i: but I must yield to grievous old age,
sentences.n: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative ἐμέ and an infinitive. πείθεσθαι with the dative γήραϊ λυγρῷ is ‘to yield to, be ruled by’. λυγρός ‘grievous’ goes with γῆρας ‘old age’ (γήραϊ is the epic dative).

sentences.t: τότε δ’ αὖτε μετέπρεπον ἡρώεσσιν.
sentences.tr: tote d’ aute meteprepon hērōessin.
sentences.l: but then, in turn, I was conspicuous among the heroes.
sentences.i: but then I stood out among the heroes.
sentences.n: τότε ‘then’ answers νῦν ‘now’, with αὖτε ‘in turn’. μετέπρεπον is the imperfect of μεταπρέπω ‘be conspicuous among’, and it takes the dative ἡρώεσσιν, the epic dative plural of ἥρως ‘hero’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴθι καὶ σὸν ἑταῖρον ἀέθλοισι κτερέϊζε.
sentences.tr: all’ ithi kai son hetairon aethloisi ktereïze.
sentences.l: But go, and render funeral rites to your companion with contests.
sentences.i: But go, and pay your companion funeral honours with contests.
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. κτερέϊζε is the imperative of κτερεΐζω ‘pay funeral rites’ (the verb of the funeral gifts, κτέρεα), and ἀέθλοισι is the dative plural of ἄεθλος ‘contest’, the means. σὸν ἑταῖρον ‘your companion’ is Patroclus. Nestor bids Achilles go on with the games.

sentences.t: τοῦτο δ’ ἐγὼ πρόφρων δέχομαι, χαίρει δέ μοι ἦτορ,
sentences.tr: touto d’ egō prophrōn dechomai, chairei de moi ētor,
sentences.l: And this I, ready-minded, accept, and my heart rejoices,
sentences.i: I accept this readily, and my heart rejoices,
sentences.n: τοῦτο ‘this’ is the bowl. πρόφρων ‘ready-minded’ (from πρό and φρήν) is a nominative adjective used like an adverb, ‘readily’. χαίρει δέ μοι ἦτορ is ‘and for me the heart rejoices’, with the dative μοι of the person affected.

sentences.t: ὥς μευ ἀεὶ μέμνησαι ἐνηέος, οὐδέ σε λήθω,
sentences.tr: hōs meu aei memnēsai enēeos, oude se lēthō,
sentences.l: that you always remember me, the kindly one, and I do not escape you,
sentences.i: that you always remember me, kindly as I am, and I do not escape your notice,
sentences.n: ὥς here is ‘how, that’, giving the reason for his joy. μέμνησαι is the perfect of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’ and takes the genitive μευ (epic for μου). ἐνηέος ‘kindly’ agrees with μευ. λήθω is λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’ with the accusative σε: he means he is not forgotten.

sentences.t: τιμῆς ἧς τέ μ’ ἔοικε τετιμῆσθαι μετ’ Ἀχαιοῖς.
sentences.tr: timēs hēs te m’ eoike tetimēsthai met’ Achaiois.
sentences.l: and of the honour with which it is fitting that I be honoured among the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and of the honour with which it is right that I be honoured among the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τιμῆς is the genitive after μέμνησαι of the line before: ‘you remember me and the honour’. ἧς is the relative, put into the genitive like its noun, and τε after it marks a general rule. ἔοικε is used impersonally, ‘it is fitting’, with the perfect passive infinitive τετιμῆσθαι ‘to be honoured’. μετ’ Ἀχαιοῖς is ‘among the Achaeans’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δὲ θεοὶ τῶνδ’ ἀντὶ χάριν μενοεικέα δοῖεν.
sentences.tr: soi de theoi tōnd’ anti charin menoeikea doien.
sentences.l: And to you may the gods in return for these things give a satisfying favour.”
sentences.i: And may the gods give you a satisfying favour in return for these things.”
sentences.n: A wish. δοῖεν is the aorist optative, third plural, of δίδωμι. τῶνδ’ ἀντί is ‘in return for these things’ (ἀντί takes the genitive). χάριν is ‘favour’, with μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’, one that fills the wish of the heart. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Πηλεΐδης δὲ πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον Ἀχαιῶν
ᾤχετ’, ἐπεὶ πάντ’ αἶνον ἐπέκλυε Νηλεΐδαο.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Pēleïdēs de polyn kath’ homilon Achaiōn
ōichet’, epei pant’ ainon epeklye Nēleïdao.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Peleus’-son through the great throng of the Achaeans
went off, when he had heard all the praise of Neleus’-son.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Peleus went off through the great throng of the Achaeans, when he had listened to all the praise of the son of Neleus.
sentences.n: Peleus’-son is Achilles, and Neleus’-son (Νηλεΐδαο, the patronymic in the epic genitive) is Nestor. πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘down through the thick throng’. ᾤχετ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’. ἐπέκλυε is the aorist of ἐπικλύω ‘hear, listen to’. αἶνος is ‘praise’, here Nestor’s speech of thanks; πάντ’ is ‘all of it’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ πυγμαχίης ἀλεγεινῆς θῆκεν ἄεθλα·
sentences.tr: autar ho pygmachiēs alegeinēs thēken aethla·
sentences.l: and he for grievous boxing set the contest-prizes;
sentences.i: and he set out prizes for the grievous boxing:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘and he’ is Achilles, back at the games. πυγμαχίης is the genitive of πυγμαχίη ‘boxing’ (from πυγμή ‘fist’ and μάχη), depending on ἄεθλα, and ἀλεγεινῆς ‘grievous’ describes it. θῆκεν is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set out’. The next lines name the two prizes.

sentences.t:
ἡμίονον ταλαεργὸν ἄγων κατέδησ’ ἐν ἀγῶνι
ἑξέτε’ ἀδμήτην, ἥ τ’ ἀλγίστη δαμάσασθαι·
sentences.tr:
hēmionon talaergon agōn katedēs’ en agōni
hexete’ admētēn, hē t’ algistē damasasthai·
sentences.l:
a mule, toil-enduring, leading, he tied up in the gathering,
six years old, untamed, which is the most painful to subdue;
sentences.i: He led up a toil-enduring mule and tied it in the gathering, six years old, unbroken, the most troublesome kind to break;
sentences.n: ἡμίονον ‘mule’; ταλαεργόν ‘toil-enduring’ is built on τλάω ‘endure’ and ἔργον ‘work’. ἄγων … κατέδησ’ is ‘leading … tied up’ (καταδέω). ἑξέτε’ is ἑξέτεα ‘six years old’. ἀδμήτην is feminine, so the mule is a female, and ἀδμής is ‘untamed’. ἥ τ’ ἀλγίστη δαμάσασθαι is a general remark: ἀλγίστη is ‘most painful’ and δαμάσασθαι ‘to subdue’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἄρα νικηθέντι τίθει δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ ara nikēthenti tithei depas amphikypellon.
sentences.l: and for the one beaten he set a double cup.
sentences.i: and for the loser he set out a double cup.
sentences.n: τῷ … νικηθέντι is ‘for him who was beaten’ (aorist passive participle of νικάω, in the dative). τίθει is the unaugmented imperfect. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is the ‘double cup’; the loser’s prize is the cup and the winner’s the mule.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ orthos kai mython en Argeioisin eeipen·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: Achilles rises to announce the boxing, and the next unit is his speech. The same line introduced his announcement of the chariot race at 23.271: ὀρθός ‘upright’ and ἔειπεν, the aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἄνδρε δύω περὶ τῶνδε κελεύομεν, ὥ περ ἀρίστω,
πὺξ μάλ’ ἀνασχομένω πεπληγέμεν·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē te kai alloi eÿknēmides Achaioi
andre dyō peri tōnde keleuomen, hō per aristō,
pyx mal’ anaschomenō peplēgemen·
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus and you other well-greaved Achaeans, we call on two men, the best of you, to raise their fists high and strike each other for these prizes;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is a singular vocative, ‘son of Atreus’, and it is not said which of the two sons is meant. ἄνδρε δύω ‘two men’, ὥ περ ἀρίστω ‘who are the best’ and ἀνασχομένω ‘raising’ (aorist participle of ἀνέχω) are all duals. κελεύομεν ‘we bid’ takes the infinitive πεπληγέμεν, the epic perfect infinitive of πλήσσω ‘strike’. περὶ τῶνδε is ‘for these things’, the prizes. πὺξ μάλ’ is ‘with the fist, strongly’.

sentences.t:
ᾧ δέ κ’ Ἀπόλλων
δώῃ καμμονίην, γνώωσι δὲ πάντες Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
hōi de k’ Apollōn
dōēi kammoniēn, gnōōsi de pantes Achaioi,
sentences.l:
and he to whom Apollo shall give
staying-power, and all the Achaeans shall know it,
sentences.i: and the man to whom Apollo gives endurance, and all the Achaeans will know it,
sentences.n: ᾧ is the relative ‘to whom’, and κε with the subjunctive δώῃ (epic for δῷ) makes it ‘whoever’. Apollo is named as the giver of καμμονίη, whose exact sense is not certain (22.257); ‘staying-power’ is the word kept. γνώωσι is the epic subjunctive of γιγνώσκω ‘know’. This relative clause is finished by the order in the next unit.

sentences.t: ἡμίονον ταλαεργὸν ἄγων κλισίην δὲ νεέσθω·
sentences.tr: hēmionon talaergon agōn klisiēn de neesthō·
sentences.l: the mule, toil-enduring, leading, to his hut let him go;
sentences.i: let him go back to his hut, leading the toil-enduring mule;
sentences.n: νεέσθω is the third-person imperative of νέομαι ‘go (back)’. κλισίην δέ is κλισίην with the ending -δε ‘to’, so ‘to the hut’; ἄγων ‘leading’ and ἡμίονον ταλαεργόν are as in 654.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ νικηθεὶς δέπας οἴσεται ἀμφικύπελλον.
sentences.tr: autar ho nikētheis depas oisetai amphikypellon.
sentences.l: but he who is beaten the double cup will carry off.”
sentences.i: but the loser will carry off the double cup.”
sentences.n: ὃ … νικηθείς is ‘he who is beaten’, the aorist passive participle, with ὁ as the pronoun. οἴσεται is the future of φέρω, ‘will carry off’. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὄρνυτο δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀνὴρ ἠΰς τε μέγας τε
εἰδὼς πυγμαχίης υἱὸς Πανοπῆος Ἐπειός,
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, ornyto d’ autik’ anēr ēÿs te megas te
eidōs pygmachiēs huios Panopēos Epeios,
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and at once there rose a man both good and great,
skilled in boxing, Epeius, son of Panopeus,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and at once a man both good and great started up, skilled in boxing, Epeius, son of Panopeus,
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατο). ὄρνυτο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘rose, started up’. ἠΰς τε μέγας τε ‘both good and great’ is a stock phrase (3.167). εἰδώς ‘knowing’ takes the genitive πυγμαχίης, ‘skilled in boxing’. Ἐπειός is a man’s name, ‘Epeius’; he is not to be taken for the people called Ἐπειοί ‘Epeans’ in Nestor’s speech.

sentences.t: ἅψατο δ’ ἡμιόνου ταλαεργοῦ φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: hapsato d’ hēmionou talaergou phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: and he laid hold of the toil-enduring mule and spoke:
sentences.i: He laid hold of the toil-enduring mule and said:
sentences.n: ἅψατο is the aorist of ἅπτομαι ‘lay hold of’, with the genitive ἡμιόνου ταλαεργοῦ, so he claims the prize before he speaks. φώνησεν is the aorist ‘spoke up’, and τε joins the two actions.

sentences.t: ἆσσον ἴτω ὅς τις δέπας οἴσεται ἀμφικύπελλον·
sentences.tr: asson itō hos tis depas oisetai amphikypellon·
sentences.l: “Let him come near, whoever will carry off the double cup;
sentences.i: “Let whoever is going to carry off the double cup come close;
sentences.n: ἆσσον is the comparative adverb ‘nearer’, and ἴτω is the imperative of εἶμι, ‘let him come’. ὅς τις (written as two words) is ‘whoever’, and οἴσεται ‘will carry off’ is the future of φέρω, as in Achilles’ words at 663. Epeius is saying that only the loser gets the cup: let someone come and be beaten.

sentences.t:
ἡμίονον δ’ οὔ φημί τιν’ ἀξέμεν ἄλλον Ἀχαιῶν
πυγμῇ νικήσαντ’,
sentences.tr:
hēmionon d’ ou phēmi tin’ axemen allon Achaiōn
pygmēi nikēsant’,
sentences.l:
but the mule, I say, no other of the Achaeans will lead away,
having won by boxing,
sentences.i: but the mule, I say, no other of the Achaeans will lead away, having won it by boxing,
sentences.n: οὔ φημι ‘I say … not’ takes the future infinitive ἀξέμεν (epic, from ἄγω) ‘will lead off’. τιν’ ἄλλον Ἀχαιῶν is ‘any other of the Achaeans’. πυγμῇ is the dative ‘by boxing’ (πυγμή ‘fist’), and νικήσαντ’ the accusative aorist participle ‘having won’.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ εὔχομαι εἶναι ἄριστος.
sentences.tr: epei euchomai einai aristos.
sentences.l: since I claim to be the best.
sentences.i: since I claim to be the best.
sentences.n: ἐπεί gives his reason. εὔχομαι with the infinitive εἶναι is ‘I claim, I boast, that I am’ (the verb also means ‘pray’), and ἄριστος is ‘best’, which is why no one else should win the mule.

sentences.t: ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ὅττι μάχης ἐπιδεύομαι;
sentences.tr: ē ouch halis hotti machēs epideuomai;
sentences.l: Is it not enough that I am lacking in battle?
sentences.i: Is it not enough that I fall short in battle?
sentences.n: ἦ introduces a question, and ἅλις is ‘enough’. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’. ἐπιδεύομαι takes the genitive of what one lacks, μάχης ‘battle’ (compare δεύεαι at 23.484). Epeius admits he is no fighter in war, and then argues that no man has every skill.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα πως ἦν
ἐν πάντεσσ’ ἔργοισι δαήμονα φῶτα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara pōs ēn
en pantess’ ergoisi daēmona phōta genesthai.
sentences.l:
Nor, then, was it in any way possible
for a man in all works to become skilled.
sentences.i: No man, after all, can ever become skilled in every kind of work.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρα πως ἦν is ‘nor then was it in any way’, where ἦν is used for ‘was possible’ and ἄρα marks something obvious. ἔργοισι is the epic dative plural of ἔργον ‘work’, and δαήμονα φῶτα is ‘a skilled man’ (δαήμων ‘knowing’; φώς ‘man’). γενέσθαι ‘to become’ is the infinitive.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.tr: hōde gar exereō, to de kai tetelesmenon estai·
sentences.l: For thus I will declare, and this too fulfilled shall be;
sentences.i: For I will say it in this way, and what I say will also be fulfilled:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ and ἐξερέω ‘I will declare’ (future of ἐξερέω) point forward to the threat. τὸ δέ ‘and this’ is what he says, and τετελεσμένον ἔσται is the future perfect ‘will have been fulfilled’. The same line stands at 1.212.

sentences.t: ἀντικρὺ χρόα τε ῥήξω σύν τ’ ὀστέ’ ἀράξω.
sentences.tr: antikry chroa te rhēxō syn t’ oste’ araxō.
sentences.l: Straight through I will break the skin and crush the bones together.
sentences.i: I will break straight through his skin and crush his bones.
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ is ‘straight through’. χρόα is the accusative of χρώς ‘skin’, and ῥήξω the future of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. σύν … ἀράξω is tmesis for συναράσσω ‘crush together’ (future), and ὀστέ’ is ὀστέα ‘bones’. ‘His’ is not in the Greek; the threat is aimed at whoever comes forward.

sentences.t: κηδεμόνες δέ οἱ ἐνθάδ’ ἀολλέες αὖθι μενόντων,
sentences.tr: kēdemones de hoi enthad’ aollees authi menontōn,
sentences.l: and let the caretakers for him here, together, on the spot stay,
sentences.i: and let those who will take care of him wait here together on the spot,
sentences.n: κηδεμόνες ‘caretakers’ (23.163) are here the people who will look after the beaten man and take him away. οἱ is ‘for him’. ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’, ἀολλέες ‘all together’, and αὖθι ‘right there’. μενόντων is the third-person plural imperative of μένω, ‘let them stay’.

sentences.t: οἵ κέ μιν ἐξοίσουσιν ἐμῇς ὑπὸ χερσὶ δαμέντα.
sentences.tr: hoi ke min exoisousin emēis hypo chersi damenta.
sentences.l: who will carry him out, subdued under my hands.”
sentences.i: who will carry him out, subdued under my hands.”
sentences.n: οἵ κε with the future ἐξοίσουσιν (ἐκφέρω ‘carry out’) says what these caretakers will do. μιν is the beaten man, and δαμέντα, the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, agrees with it. ὑπὸ χερσί is ‘under the hands’. Epeius’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: A stock line: the boast is answered by silence. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is ‘became still in silence’, with the adverb ἀκήν ‘still’ and the dative σιωπῇ.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύαλος δέ οἱ οἶος ἀνίστατο ἰσόθεος φὼς
Μηκιστῆος υἱὸς Ταλαϊονίδαο ἄνακτος,
sentences.tr:
Euryalos de hoi oios anistato isotheos phōs
Mēkistēos huios Talaïonidao anaktos,
sentences.l:
But Euryalus alone stood up against him, a man equal to a god,
son of Mecisteus, the lord, Talaion’s descendant,
sentences.i: But only Euryalus stood up against him, a man the equal of a god, the son of the lord Mecisteus, a descendant of Talaion,
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘against him’ and οἶος ‘alone’, so Euryalus is the only one who answers. ἀνίστατο is the imperfect middle of ἀνίσταμαι ‘stand up’. ἰσόθεος φώς is ‘a man equal to a god’. Μηκιστῆος and Ταλαϊονίδαο ἄνακτος are both genitives after υἱός and name the same man: Mecisteus, the lord, a descendant of Talaion (Ταλαϊονίδης is a patronymic like Ἀτρεΐδης).

sentences.t:
ὅς ποτε Θήβας δ’ ἦλθε δεδουπότος Οἰδιπόδαο
ἐς τάφον·
sentences.tr:
hos pote Thēbas d’ ēlthe dedoupotos Oidipodao
es taphon·
sentences.l:
who once to Thebes came, Oedipus having fallen,
to the burial;
sentences.i: who once went to Thebes, after Oedipus had fallen, for his burial;
sentences.n: Θήβας δ’ is Θήβας with -δε ‘to’, so ‘to Thebes’. δεδουπότος Οἰδιπόδαο is a genitive absolute, ‘Oedipus having fallen’; δεδουπότος is the perfect participle of δουπέω ‘fall with a thud’, and here it means that he had died. ἐς τάφον is ‘to the burial’. The burial brought a contest.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ πάντας ἐνίκα Καδμείωνας.
sentences.tr: entha de pantas enika Kadmeiōnas.
sentences.l: and there he kept prevailing over all the Cadmeans.
sentences.i: and there he kept defeating all the Cadmeans.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’, at the burial. ἐνίκα is the imperfect of νικάω, ‘kept winning’, so he beat every challenger. Καδμείωνας ‘Cadmeans’ are the people of Thebes.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Τυδεΐδης δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἀμφεπονεῖτο
θαρσύνων ἔπεσιν, μέγα δ’ αὐτῷ βούλετο νίκην.
sentences.tr:
ton men Tydeïdēs douri klytos ampheponeito
tharsynōn epesin, mega d’ autōi bouleto nikēn.
sentences.l:
Him Tydeus’-son, famous with the spear, busied himself about,
cheering him with words, and greatly for him wanted victory.
sentences.i: The son of Tydeus, famous with the spear, busied himself about him, cheering him on with words, and wanted the victory for him very much.
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him’ is Euryalus, and Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes, not named. ἀμφεπονεῖτο is the imperfect of ἀμφιπονέομαι ‘busy oneself about, tend’. δουρὶ κλυτός is ‘famous with the spear’. θαρσύνων is ‘cheering’, and ἔπεσιν is the dative plural ‘with words’. μέγα … βούλετο νίκην is ‘greatly wanted victory’, αὐτῷ ‘for him’.

sentences.t:
ζῶμα δέ οἱ πρῶτον παρακάββαλεν, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
δῶκεν ἱμάντας ἐϋτμήτους βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο.
sentences.tr:
zōma de hoi prōton parakabbalen, autar epeita
dōken himantas eÿtmētous boos agrauloio.
sentences.l:
The waistcloth first he laid down beside him, and then
gave him well-cut straps of a field-dwelling ox.
sentences.i: First he laid a waistcloth down beside him, and then gave him well-cut straps from an ox of the fields.
sentences.n: ζῶμα is the ‘waistcloth’ (4.187). παρακάββαλεν is παρακατέβαλεν (παρά ‘beside’, κατά ‘down’, and βάλλω), ‘laid down beside’, with οἱ ‘for him’. ἱμάντας ‘straps’ are the boxer’s binding, and ἐϋτμήτους (printed with the diaeresis) is ‘well-cut’. βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο is ‘of an ox living in the fields’; ἀγραύλοιο is built on ἀγρός ‘field’ and, probably, αὐλή ‘dwelling-place’.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ ζωσαμένω βήτην ἐς μέσσον ἀγῶνα,
sentences.tr: tō de zōsamenō bētēn es messon agōna,
sentences.l: And the two, having girded themselves, went into the middle of the gathering,
sentences.i: The two girded themselves and went into the middle of the gathering,
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article ‘the two’, and ζωσαμένω the dual aorist participle of ζώννυμι ‘gird’; βήτην is the dual aorist of βαίνω ‘went’. ἐς μέσσον ἀγῶνα is ‘into the middle of the gathering’, the open space among the seated people (they sit down in it at 23.258).

sentences.t:
ἄντα δ’ ἀνασχομένω χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν ἅμ’ ἄμφω
σύν ῥ’ ἔπεσον, σὺν δέ σφι βαρεῖαι χεῖρες ἔμιχθεν.
sentences.tr:
anta d’ anaschomenō chersi stibarēisin ham’ amphō
syn rh’ epeson, syn de sphi bareiai cheires emichthen.
sentences.l:
Face to face, both together raising their stout hands,
they fell together, and together for them heavy hands were mingled.
sentences.i: Facing each other, they raised their stout hands, both together, and came together, and their heavy hands were mingled.
sentences.n: ἄντα is ‘face to face’, and ἀνασχομένω is the dual participle again (as at 660). χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν is ‘with stout hands’ (the epic dative plural -ῃσιν), ἅμ’ ἄμφω ‘both together’. σύν … ἔπεσον is tmesis for συνέπεσον ‘fell in together, clashed’, and ῥ’ is ῥα. σὺν δέ … ἔμιχθεν is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, ‘were mingled’, with σφι ‘for them’.

sentences.t:
δεινὸς δὲ χρόμαδος γενύων γένετ’, ἔρρεε δ’ ἱδρὼς
πάντοθεν ἐκ μελέων·
sentences.tr:
deinos de chromados genyōn genet’, erree d’ hidrōs
pantothen ek meleōn·
sentences.l:
And a dreadful grinding of jaws arose, and sweat flowed
from everywhere out of their limbs;
sentences.i: A dreadful grinding of jaws arose, and sweat ran from their limbs on every side;
sentences.n: χρόμαδος is a rare noun, a grinding or crunching sound, and the English follows the context. γενύων is the genitive plural of γένυς ‘jaw’. ἔρρεε is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’, and πάντοθεν ‘from all sides’ goes with ἐκ μελέων ‘out of the limbs’ (μέλος).

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ὄρνυτο δῖος Ἐπειός,
κόψε δὲ παπτήναντα παρήϊον·
sentences.tr:
epi d’ ornyto dios Epeios,
kopse de paptēnanta parēïon·
sentences.l:
and upon him started up heavenly Epeius,
and struck him on the cheek as he glanced about;
sentences.i: and heavenly Epeius started up at him and struck him on the cheek as he glanced about;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ὄρνυτο is tmesis, ‘started up against’. δῖος Ἐπειός is ‘heavenly Epeius’. κόψε is the aorist of κόπτω ‘strike’, with two accusatives, the man struck (παπτήναντα, the aorist participle of παπταίνω ‘glance about’, which is Euryalus) and the part struck (παρήϊον ‘cheek’).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
ἑστήκειν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ eti dēn
hestēkein·
sentences.l:
and not then any more for long
was he standing;
sentences.i: and he did not go on standing for long;
sentences.n: ἑστήκειν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, used with the sense of an imperfect, ‘was standing’. ἔτι δήν is ‘still for long’, and οὐδ’ ἄρα ‘and not, as it turned out’.

sentences.t: αὐτοῦ γὰρ ὑπήριπε φαίδιμα γυῖα.
sentences.tr: autou gar hypēripe phaidima guia.
sentences.l: for on the spot his glorious limbs gave way beneath him.
sentences.i: for his glorious limbs gave way beneath him on the spot.
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is an adverb ‘on the very spot’ (not the pronoun). ὑπήριπε is ὑπο- ‘under’ and the aorist ἤριπε of ἐρείπω ‘fall, collapse’, ‘gave way beneath’. φαίδιμα γυῖα is ‘glorious limbs’, the stock phrase.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ὑπὸ φρικὸς Βορέω ἀναπάλλεται ἰχθὺς
θίν’ ἐν φυκιόεντι, μέλαν δέ ἑ κῦμα κάλυψεν,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hoth’ hypo phrikos Boreō anapalletai ichthys
thin’ en phykioenti, melan de he kyma kalypsen,
sentences.l:
And as when under the ripple of the North Wind a fish leaps up
on the weedy shore, and a dark wave covered it,
sentences.i: As when, under the North Wind’s ripple, a fish leaps up on the weedy shore, and a dark wave covers it,
sentences.n: A simile for the blow. φρικός is the genitive of φρίξ ‘ripple, shudder on the water’, with ὑπό, and Βορέω is the epic genitive of Βορέης ‘North Wind’. ἀναπάλλεται ‘leaps up’ is the present middle of ἀναπάλλω, the verb that appears again in the next line. θίν’ is the dative θῖνι ‘shore’ with its final vowel dropped, and φυκιόεντι ‘weedy’ is from φῦκος ‘seaweed’. ἑ is ‘it’. The aorist κάλυψεν, in a simile, states what happens, and English uses the present.

sentences.t: ὣς πληγεὶς ἀνέπαλτ’·
sentences.tr: hōs plēgeis anepalt’·
sentences.l: so, struck, he leapt up;
sentences.i: so, struck, he leapt up;
sentences.n: ὥς closes the simile. πληγείς is the aorist passive participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’. ἀνέπαλτ’ is ἀνέπαλτο, the aorist of ἀναπάλλομαι ‘leap up’, the same verb as in the simile. The Greek does not say whether he springs up of himself or is jerked up by the blow, like the fish.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ μεγάθυμος Ἐπειὸς
χερσὶ λαβὼν ὤρθωσε·
sentences.tr:
autar megathymos Epeios
chersi labōn ōrthōse·
sentences.l:
but great-hearted Epeius,
taking him in his hands, set him upright;
sentences.i: but great-hearted Epeius took him in his hands and set him upright;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from the stricken man to the winner, μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’. χερσὶ λαβών is ‘taking in his hands’, and ὤρθωσε the aorist of ὀρθόω ‘set upright, raise’.

sentences.t: φίλοι δ’ ἀμφέσταν ἑταῖροι,
sentences.tr: philoi d’ amphestan hetairoi,
sentences.l: and dear companions stood around him,
sentences.i: and his dear companions stood around him,
sentences.n: ἀμφέσταν is ἀμφέστησαν, the short-form aorist of ἀμφίστημι ‘stand around’. φίλοι ἑταῖροι are ‘dear companions’, the friends of the beaten man; the next unit goes on about what they did.

sentences.t:
οἵ μιν ἄγον δι’ ἀγῶνος ἐφελκομένοισι πόδεσσιν
αἷμα παχὺ πτύοντα κάρη βάλλονθ’ ἑτέρωσε·
sentences.tr:
hoi min agon di’ agōnos ephelkomenoisi podessin
haima pachy ptyonta karē ballonth’ heterōse·
sentences.l:
who led him through the gathering with feet dragging,
spitting thick blood, his head throwing to the other side;
sentences.i: and they led him through the gathering with his feet dragging, spitting thick blood, his head dropping to the other side;
sentences.n: οἵ is the relative, ‘who’, the companions. ἄγον is the imperfect ‘led’, and δι’ ἀγῶνος ‘through the gathering’. ἐφελκομένοισι πόδεσσιν is ‘with feet dragging’ (the dative plural of the middle participle of ἐφέλκω). πτύοντα ‘spitting’ and βάλλονθ’ (elided βάλλοντα) both agree with μιν; κάρη is ‘head’, and βάλλω here is ‘let drop’. ἑτέρωσε is ‘to the other side’.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἀλλοφρονέοντα μετὰ σφίσιν εἷσαν ἄγοντες,
sentences.tr: kad d’ allophroneonta meta sphisin heisan agontes,
sentences.l: and, thinking elsewhere, among themselves they sat him down, leading him,
sentences.i: and, with his thoughts elsewhere, they led him in and sat him down among them,
sentences.n: κὰδ … εἷσαν is tmesis: κατά ‘down’ (written κὰδ before δ) with the aorist εἷσαν of ἵζω ‘seat’, ‘sat him down’. ἀλλοφρονέοντα ‘thinking elsewhere’ means dazed. μετὰ σφίσιν is ‘among themselves’, and ἄγοντες ‘leading’.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δ’ οἰχόμενοι κόμισαν δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον.
sentences.tr: autoi d’ oichomenoi komisan depas amphikypellon.
sentences.l: and they themselves, going off, carried away the double cup.
sentences.i: and they themselves went off and carried away the double cup.
sentences.n: αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ sets the companions’ errand against the dazed man sitting where they put him. οἰχόμενοι is ‘going off’ (οἴχομαι, as at 652), and κόμισαν is the aorist of κομίζω ‘carry off’. The double cup is the loser’s prize named at 656, and 663 says the loser carries it off. The part ends here.
